---
title: "Bayes: Read the Same Evidence in Reverse"
---

A detector is good at flagging faulty items. An item has been flagged.

These sentences look close enough to invite a shortcut. But the first starts from faults and asks about flags. The second starts from flags and asks about faults.

We need to keep both kinds of item in view.

## 🔰 Count the routes to a flag {#sec-sample-bayes-count-the-routes-to-a-flag}

Use the numerical assumptions from the presentation in a hypothetical factory:

- One item in a thousand is faulty.
- The detector flags 99% of faulty items.
- It also flags 2% of fault-free items.

In a hypothetical group of 100,000 items, the expected counts are:

- 100 faulty items: 99 flagged and 1 unflagged.
- 99,900 fault-free items: 1,998 flagged and 97,902 unflagged.

These are model-based expected counts; a finite observed batch can differ.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sample-bayes-counts
%%| fig-cap: "Expected counts under the stated detector model. The flagged population receives items through two different routes."
flowchart TD
    U["100,000 items"] --> F["100 faulty"]
    U --> N["99,900 fault-free"]
    F --> TP["99 flagged"]
    F --> FN["1 unflagged"]
    N --> FP["1,998 flagged"]
    N --> TN["97,902 unflagged"]
```

## 🏵 Read within the population selected by the evidence {#sec-sample-bayes-read-within-the-population-selected-by-the-evidence}

The flag retains $99+1998=2097$ items in this expected-count picture. Of those, 99 are faulty.

Thus

$$
\mathbb P(\text{fault}\mid\text{flag})
=
\frac{99}{2097}
\approx0.0472.
$$

The 99% figure described flags among faults. The 4.72% figure describes faults among flags.

Both are correct under the model because they use different reference populations.

## ⚙️ Derive the reversal from the joint event {#sec-sample-bayes-derive-the-reversal-from-the-joint-event}

Let $F$ mean fault and $E$ mean evidence.

The probability of their intersection can be read in either order:

$$
\mathbb P(F\cap E)
=
\mathbb P(E\mid F)\mathbb P(F)
=
\mathbb P(F\mid E)\mathbb P(E).
$$

When the conditioning events have positive probability, rearranging gives

$$
\mathbb P(F\mid E)
=
\frac{\mathbb P(E\mid F)\mathbb P(F)}
     {\mathbb P(E)}.
$$

The denominator includes every route to the evidence. In this binary example,

$$
\mathbb P(E)
=
\mathbb P(E\mid F)\mathbb P(F)
+
\mathbb P(E\mid F^c)\mathbb P(F^c).
$$

Bayes' rule is conditioning viewed from the other direction.

## 💡 Evidence has strength within a background {#sec-sample-bayes-evidence-has-strength-within-a-background}

Keep the same detector but imagine half the incoming items are faulty. The conditional probability of a fault after a flag becomes

$$
\frac{0.99(0.5)}
     {0.99(0.5)+0.02(0.5)}
=
\frac{99}{101}
\approx0.9802.
$$

The detector's conditional rates stayed fixed. The incoming mixture changed.

A flag does not carry one universal probability of fault independently of the population where it is used.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-bayes-try-the-idea}

With the original assumptions, a batch is screened twice. Can we calculate the probability of two flags on a fault-free item as $0.02^2$ from the given facts alone?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-bayes-work-it-through}

No. We also need the relationship between the repeated detector results. Squaring requires conditional independence of the two flags for fault-free items under the relevant model. Repeating a measurement can repeat the same source of error.
:::
